then.say: You come to a complete stop, look both ways, and go when it is safe. A flashing red light means the same as a stop sign. You stop every time, even when no other car is in sight, and you do not wait for a green light.

wrong.You slow down and go through without sto: A flashing red light means the same as a stop sign, so you stop every time, even when no other car is in sight. You come to a complete stop, look both ways, and go when it is safe.
wrong.You stop and wait until the light turns: A flashing red light means the same as a stop sign, so after a complete stop you do not wait for a green light. You look both ways and go when it is safe.

steps.rule: A flashing red light means you come to a complete stop, the same as at a stop sign, then look both ways and go when it is safe.

steps.prompt: You are coming up to a flashing yellow light and want to drive straight across. No other car is in sight. What do you do?
options: You slow down and drive through with care.
You come to a complete stop, the same as at a stop sign.
You speed up to get through the intersection.
steps.answer: You slow down and drive through with care.

then.say: You slow down and drive through with care. A flashing yellow light tells you to slow down and take care, but not to stop. A flashing red light is the one that means the same as a stop sign.

wrong.You come to a complete stop, the same as: That is what a flashing red light means. A flashing yellow light tells you to slow down and take care, but not to stop, so you slow down and drive through with care.
wrong.You speed up to get through the intersec: A flashing yellow light tells you to slow down and take care, and speeding up does the opposite. You slow down and drive through with care.

steps.rule: A flashing yellow light means you slow down and drive through the intersection with care.

steps.prompt: You stopped for the steady yellow light. You slowed down and drove through the flashing yellow light. What is the difference between a steady yellow light and a flashing yellow light?
options: A steady yellow light is about to turn red, and a flashing yellow light is not.
A flashing yellow light is about to turn red, and a steady yellow light is not.
They mean the same thing, and the flashing only makes the light easier to see.
steps.answer: A steady yellow light is about to turn red, and a flashing yellow light is not.

then.say: A steady yellow light is about to turn red, and a flashing yellow light is not. That is why you stop for a steady yellow light when you safely can, and slow down and drive through a flashing yellow light with care.

wrong.A flashing yellow light is about to turn: You stopped for the steady yellow light because it is about to turn red. A flashing yellow light is not about to turn red, so you slowed down and drove through it with care.
wrong.They mean the same thing, and the flashi: You stopped for the steady yellow light and drove through the flashing yellow light, so they do not mean the same thing. A steady yellow light is about to turn red, and a flashing yellow light is not.

steps.rule: A steady yellow light is about to turn red, so you stop when you safely can, while a flashing yellow light is not about to change and means slow down and drive through with care.

steps.prompt: The arrow over your lane is a steady green left arrow, and you want to turn left. The light over the lane beside you, for cars going straight, is a red light. On the other side of the intersection, a car facing you is stopped. Who goes first? Tap the car.

then.say: Your car goes first. The green arrow lets you turn left now, and the car facing you waits until you have turned. You still wait for any car or person already in the intersection.

wrong.oncoming: The car facing you is stopped, and the green arrow over your lane lets you turn left now. Your car goes first, after any car or person already in the intersection, and the car facing you waits until you have turned.

steps.rule: A green arrow means you may turn only in the arrow's direction and the other traffic waits for you, after any vehicles and people already in the intersection have cleared it.

steps.prompt: You want to turn left. The green arrow over your lane has just changed to a steady yellow arrow. The light over the lane beside you is a red light. You can still stop safely before the intersection. On the other side of the intersection, a car facing you is stopped. What do you do?
options: You slow down and stop before the intersection.
You go on and turn now.
You speed up to turn before the arrow turns red.
steps.answer: You slow down and stop before the intersection.

then.say: You slow down and stop before the intersection. A yellow arrow means your turn is ending and the cars coming toward you will soon get to go, so you get ready to let them go first. You never speed up to turn before the arrow turns red.

A steady yellow arrow means your turn is ending, and the cars coming toward you will soon get to go. You can still stop safely, so you slow down and stop before the intersection.
wrong.You speed up to turn before the arrow tu: A steady yellow arrow means your turn is ending, and you never speed up to turn before the arrow turns red. You can still stop safely, so you slow down and stop before the intersection.

steps.rule: A yellow arrow means your protected turn is ending, so you get ready to let the oncoming traffic go first.

steps.prompt: The arrow over your lane is a flashing yellow left arrow, and you want to turn left. The light over the lane beside you, for cars going straight, is a green light. A car coming toward you is going straight across, and it is close. Who goes first? Tap the car.

then.say: The car coming toward you goes first. A flashing yellow arrow lets you turn left only after the cars coming toward you have passed and any person crossing the road has crossed. You wait for a safe gap, then turn.

wrong.you: A flashing yellow arrow lets you turn left only after the cars coming toward you have passed, so the car coming toward you goes first. You wait for a safe gap, then turn.

steps.rule: A flashing yellow arrow means you may turn left after you yield to all oncoming traffic and to bicyclists and pedestrians in the crosswalk, when there is a safe gap.

steps.prompt: You want to turn left. The arrow over your left-turn lane is a steady red arrow. The light over the lane beside you, for cars going straight, is a green light. No car and no person is in the intersection or coming toward it. May you turn left now?
options: Yes
No

then.say: No, you stop and wait until the arrow over your lane lets you turn. A red arrow means you may not turn, even when the other lanes have a green light and nothing is coming.

wrong.Yes: The green light is for the lane beside you, going straight. The arrow over your lane is a steady red arrow, and you may not turn on it, even when nothing is coming. You stop and wait until the arrow over your lane lets you turn.

steps.rule: When the arrow is red or your lane has the red light, every turn is prohibited, even when other lanes have a green light and the path looks clear.

steps.prompt: You are driving on a road with two lanes. The line down the middle of the road is solid yellow. What does the yellow line tell you?
options: The cars on the other side of the line are coming toward you.
The cars on the other side of the line are going the same way as you.
steps.answer: The cars on the other side of the line are coming toward you.

then.say: The cars on the other side of the line are coming toward you. A yellow line down the middle of a road separates traffic going in opposite directions.

wrong.The cars on the other side of the line a: Lines between lanes going the same way are white, not yellow. A yellow line separates traffic going in opposite directions, so the cars on the other side of it are coming toward you.

steps.rule: Lines that separate traffic moving in opposite directions are yellow.

steps.prompt: You are driving on a road with two lanes. The line between your lane and the lane next to you is white and broken. What does the white line tell you?
options: The cars in the lane next to you are going the same way as you.
The cars in the lane next to you are coming toward you.
You may never cross the line.
steps.answer: The cars in the lane next to you are going the same way as you.

then.say: The cars in the lane next to you are going the same way as you. White lines separate lanes of traffic going the same way. You may cross a broken white line to change lanes when it is safe.

wrong.The cars in the lane next to you are com: Lines between traffic going in opposite directions are yellow, not white. A white line separates lanes going the same way, so the cars in the lane next to you are going the same way as you.
You may cross a broken white line to change lanes when it is safe. It separates lanes going the same way, so the cars in the lane next to you are going the same way as you.

steps.rule: White lane markings separate lanes of traffic going in the same direction.

steps.prompt: The center of this road has a solid yellow line and a broken yellow line. The broken line is on your side. A slow car is ahead of you in your lane, and no car is coming toward you. May you pass it?
options: Yes
No

then.say: Yes, you may pass when it is safe. The broken yellow line on your side means you are in the passing zone. You must be back on your side of the road before the passing zone ends.

wrong.No: The broken yellow line is on your side, so you are in the passing zone, and no car is coming toward you. You may pass when it is safe, and you must be back on your side of the road before the passing zone ends.

steps.rule: Where the center has a solid and a broken yellow line, you may pass when the broken line is on your side and it is safe.

steps.prompt: The center of this road has a solid yellow line and a broken yellow line. The solid line is on your side. A slow car is ahead of you in your lane, and no car is coming toward you. May you pass it?
options: Yes
No

then.say: No, you stay behind the slow car. The solid yellow line on your side means you may not pass here, even when no car is coming toward you.

wrong.Yes: The solid yellow line is on your side, and that means you may not pass here, even when no car is coming toward you. You stay behind the slow car.

steps.rule: Where the center has a solid and a broken yellow line, you may not pass when the solid line is on your side.

steps.prompt: Every question in this lesson came down to one thing. What was it?
options: What the light or the line showed told you what to do.
A sign beside the road told you what to do.
How fast the other cars were going told you what to do.
steps.answer: What the light or the line showed told you what to do.

then.say: What the light or the line showed told you what to do. Red stops you, yellow tells you to take care or that a change is coming, and green lets you go when it is safe. A yellow line has cars coming toward you beyond it, a white line has cars going your way, and you pass only when the line on your side is broken.

wrong.A sign beside the road told you what to: There was no sign in this lesson. The steady and flashing lights, the arrows over your lane, and the yellow and white lines told you what to do.
wrong.How fast the other cars were going told: Behind the slow car, the broken yellow line on your side let you pass, and the solid line on your side kept you behind it. The car was slow each time, so the line decided, not the car's speed. What the light or the line showed told you what to do.

steps.prompt: You are driving out of a driveway and want to turn right onto the main road. There is no sign at the end of the driveway. A car on the main road is coming from your left and is close to the driveway. Who goes first? Tap the car.

targets.label: the car on the main road

then.say: The car on the main road goes first. You are driving onto the main road from a driveway, so you wait and let the car pass.

wrong.you: A car coming out of a driveway waits for every car already on the main road, even with no sign at the end of the driveway. The car on the main road goes first, so you wait and let it pass.

steps.rule: When you enter a main road from a driveway, an alley, a parking lot or the roadside, you yield to all vehicles already on the main road.

steps.prompt: Your road ends at a main road. There is no stop sign and no yield sign. You want to turn left onto the main road. A car on the main road is coming from your right and is close. Who goes first? Tap the car.

targets.label: the car coming from your right

then.say: The car on the main road goes first. Your road ends at the main road, so you wait for the traffic from both directions on it, even when no sign tells you to.

wrong.you: Your road ends at the main road, so you wait for the traffic from both directions on it, even when no sign tells you to. The car coming from your right goes first, so you wait and let it pass.

steps.rule: At a T intersection, the vehicles on the road that ends yield to the traffic from both directions on the main road.

steps.prompt: When you drove out of the driveway onto the main road, and when your road ended at the main road with no sign, who waited each time?
options: You did, because you were entering a road that other cars were already on.
The cars on the main road did, because they slowed down to let you in.
No one did, because the faster car went first.
steps.answer: You did, because you were entering a road that other cars were already on.

then.say: Each time, you were driving onto a main road, so you waited and let the traffic already on it go first. The law does not give anyone the right-of-way. It only says who must wait.

wrong.The cars on the main road did, because t: When you drove out of the driveway and when your road ended at the main road, the cars on the main road kept going and you waited. You were entering a road that other cars were already on, so you let them go first.
wrong.No one did, because the faster car went: Out of the driveway and at the end of your road, you waited, and how fast each car was did not decide it. You waited because you were entering a road that other cars were already on.

steps.prompt: The light ahead of you has just turned green, and you want to drive straight across. A car from your left entered the intersection before the light turned green, and it is still in the intersection. Who goes first? Tap the car.

then.say: The car in the intersection goes first. It was there before the light turned green, so you wait until it is out of the intersection before you go.

wrong.you: A green light lets you go only when the intersection is clear, and the car from your left is still in it. The car in the intersection goes first, so you wait until it is out of the intersection before you go.

steps.rule: When the light turns green, you still yield to pedestrians and vehicles that are still in the intersection.

steps.prompt: You are coming up to a steady green light, not a green arrow, and you want to turn left. A car on the other side of the intersection is coming toward you. It is going straight across, and it is close. Who goes first? Tap the car.

then.say: The car coming toward you goes first. The green light lets you go, but your left turn crosses its path, so you wait and let it pass.

wrong.you: A steady green light, not an arrow, lets you go, but your left turn crosses the path of the car coming toward you. That car goes first, so you wait and let it pass.

steps.rule: When you turn left on a green light that is not an arrow, you yield to oncoming vehicles.

steps.prompt: This is an all-way stop. Every corner has a stop sign with an ALL WAY sign under it. The car on your left stopped at the intersection before you got there. You both want to drive straight across. Who goes first? Tap the car.

then.say: The car on your left goes first. It stopped at the intersection before you did, so you stay stopped until it has gone across.

wrong.you: At an all-way stop, the car that stopped first goes first, and the car on your left stopped before you got there. You stay stopped until it has gone across.

steps.rule: At an all-way stop, every vehicle stops, and the vehicle that reached the intersection first goes first.

steps.prompt: This is an all-way stop. Every corner has a stop sign with an ALL WAY sign under it. You and the car on your right stop at the same time. You both want to drive straight across. Who goes first? Tap the car.

then.say: The car on your right goes first. You both stopped at the same time, and when that happens the car on the right goes first. You go after it.

wrong.you: You and the car on your right stopped at the same time, and when that happens at an all-way stop, the car on the right goes first. You stay stopped until the car on your right has gone across.

steps.rule: When two vehicles reach an all-way stop at the same time, the vehicle on the right goes first.

steps.prompt: The traffic light at this intersection is not working. It is dark and shows no color, and there is no stop sign. The car on your left stopped at the intersection before you got there. You both want to drive straight across. Who goes first? Tap the car.

then.say: The car on your left goes first. A traffic light that is not working makes the intersection an all-way stop. Every car stops, and the car that stopped first goes first.

wrong.you: A traffic light that is not working makes the intersection an all-way stop, so the car that stopped first goes first. The car on your left stopped before you got there, so you stay stopped until it has gone across.

steps.rule: When a traffic signal is not working, you treat the intersection as an all-way stop.

steps.prompt: This street has no traffic light and no sign. A person is standing at the side of the road on your right, at one end of the crosswalk, about to walk across. Who goes first? Tap the person or your car.

then.say: The person goes first. When a person is in a crosswalk or about to walk into it, you stop before the crosswalk and wait until the person has crossed.

wrong.you: A person about to walk into a crosswalk goes first, just as a person already in it does. You stop before the crosswalk and wait until the person has crossed.

steps.rule: You yield to pedestrians who are in a crosswalk or the street, or about to enter it, whether or not the crosswalk is marked.

steps.prompt: A person carrying a white cane with a red tip is crossing the street ahead of you, where there is no crosswalk. Must you stop and let the person cross?
options: Yes
No

then.say: Yes, you stop and wait until the person has crossed. You always stop for a person who carries a white cane, even where there is no crosswalk.

wrong.No: You always stop for a person carrying a white cane, even where there is no crosswalk. You stop and wait until the person has crossed.

steps.rule: You always yield to a blind pedestrian who carries a white cane, including a white cane with a red tip, or who uses a guide dog.

steps.prompt: You are coming up to a green light and want to drive straight across. Two cars are stopped in your lane just past the intersection, and there is no room for your car behind them. May you drive into the intersection now?
options: Yes
No

then.say: No, you stop before you enter the intersection and wait until there is room for your car past it. You enter only when you can get all the way across without stopping. A car stopped in the intersection blocks other traffic, even when its light is green.

wrong.Yes: With no room past the intersection, your car would stop inside it and block other traffic, even on a green light. You stop before the intersection and wait until there is room for your car past it.

steps.rule: You may enter an intersection only when you can get all the way through it without stopping.

steps.prompt: Every question in this lesson came down to one thing. What was it?
options: Who must wait?
Who is driving the faster car?
Which road is the bigger road?

then.say: Every right-of-way rule tells you who must wait. When that is you, you let the other driver or the person on foot go first.

wrong.Who is driving the faster car?: When the car on your left stopped first at the all-way stop, it went first, and how fast it was did not matter. Every right-of-way rule tells you who must wait.
wrong.Which road is the bigger road?: When the person was about to walk across the crosswalk, there was only one road, and you still waited. Every right-of-way rule tells you who must wait.

steps.prompt: You are driving on an interstate highway in Tennessee. No speed limit sign is posted on this stretch. It is a clear day, and the road is dry. What is the fastest Tennessee law lets you drive here?
options: The fastest is 70 mph.
The fastest is 65 mph.
The fastest is 75 mph.

then.say: The fastest is 70 mph. That is the most Tennessee law allows on an interstate, and you drive that fast only when the conditions are ideal. Some stretches of interstate have a lower posted limit.

A stretch of interstate can have a lower posted limit, but no sign posts one here. The fastest Tennessee law lets you drive here is 70 mph, and you drive that fast only when the conditions are ideal.
75 mph is faster than Tennessee law allows on any interstate. The fastest is 70 mph, and you drive that fast only when the conditions are ideal.

steps.rule: The maximum speed set by Tennessee law for interstate highways is 70 mph, to be driven only in ideal conditions, and some stretches have a lower posted limit.

steps.prompt: You are driving on a state highway with one lane each way. No speed limit sign is posted on this stretch. It is a clear day, and the road is dry. What is the fastest Tennessee law lets you drive here?
options: The fastest is 55 mph.
The fastest is 45 mph.
The fastest is 70 mph.

then.say: The fastest is 55 mph. Unless another speed is posted, the speed limit on primary and secondary state and federal highways is 55 mph. The 70 mph limit is set for interstates, and this road is not one.

45 mph would be the limit here only if a sign posted it, and no sign does. Unless another speed is posted, the speed limit on a state highway is 55 mph.
70 mph is the limit set for interstates, and this road is not one. Unless another speed is posted, the speed limit on a state highway is 55 mph.

steps.rule: Unless another speed is posted, the speed limit on primary and secondary state and federal highways is 55 mph.

steps.prompt: You are driving at night on a state highway with one lane each way. A sign says the speed limit is 55 mph. It is raining, and you cannot see far ahead. How fast do you drive?
options: You drive slower than 55 mph, at a speed that is safe in the rain and the dark.
You drive at 55 mph, because that is the posted limit.
You drive faster than 55 mph, to get out of the rain sooner.
steps.answer: You drive slower than 55 mph, at a speed that is safe in the rain and the dark.

then.say: You drive slower than 55 mph, at a speed that is safe in the rain and the dark. The Basic Speed Rule says you drive at a speed that is safe for the conditions. The posted limit is only the most the law allows, not a speed that is always safe.

wrong.You drive at 55 mph, because that is the: The posted limit is only the most the law allows, not a speed that is always safe. In the rain and the dark you cannot see far ahead, so you drive slower than 55 mph, at a speed that is safe for the conditions.
wrong.You drive faster than 55 mph, to get out: Faster than 55 mph is over the posted limit, and the rain and the dark already make 55 mph too fast to be safe. You drive slower than 55 mph, at a speed that is safe in the rain and the dark.

steps.rule: The Basic Speed Rule teaches that you drive at a speed that is safe for the conditions, even when that is slower than the posted limit.

steps.prompt: On the interstate with no sign, on the state highway with no sign, and on the state highway in rain at night, what set the fastest you should drive?
options: The speed limit set the most, and the conditions could only lower the speed you may drive, never raise it.
The speed of the cars around you set it.
How fast your car can go set it.
steps.answer: The speed limit set the most, and the conditions could only lower the speed you may drive, never raise it.

then.say: The speed limit is the most you may drive on any road, even on a dry, clear day. A law or a sign cannot know when it is raining or dark, so you judge the conditions yourself and drive slower.

The cars around you did not set it. With no sign, the law set the most, 70 mph on the interstate and 55 mph on the state highway. In the rain at night, the conditions lowered the speed you should drive below 55 mph.
How fast your car can go did not set it. With no sign, the law set the most, 70 mph on the interstate and 55 mph on the state highway. In the rain at night, the conditions lowered the speed you should drive below 55 mph.

steps.prompt: You are following a car on a state highway. The car ahead passed a sign post at the side of the road. You said “one-thousand and one, one-thousand and two” to yourself, and then your car passed the same sign post. How far behind the car ahead are you?
options: You are two seconds behind it.
You are two car lengths behind it.
You cannot tell from this.
steps.answer: You are two seconds behind it.

then.say: You are two seconds behind it. Both cars passed the same sign post, and two seconds went by between them, so the gap between you is two seconds. This is how drivers measure their following distance, by counting the seconds between the car ahead passing a fixed point and their own car reaching it.

You counted the seconds between the car ahead passing the sign post and your car passing it, and a count of seconds tells you time, not car lengths. You are two seconds behind it.
Both cars passed the same sign post, and you counted the seconds between them, so the count tells you the gap. You are two seconds behind it.

steps.rule: To check your following distance, you count the seconds from when the car ahead passes a fixed point, such as a sign post, until you reach the same point.

steps.prompt: You are following a car on a state highway on a dry day. The car ahead passed a sign post at the side of the road, and you started counting. Your car reached the sign post before you finished saying “one-thousand and two.” What do you do?
options: You slow down until you are at least two seconds behind.
You keep the same distance, because one second is enough.
You speed up to stay close to the car ahead.
steps.answer: You slow down until you are at least two seconds behind.

then.say: You slow down until you are at least two seconds behind. You reached the sign post in less than two seconds, so you were following too closely. After you slow down, you count again at another sign post or pole, until you finish “one-thousand and two” before you reach it.

wrong.You keep the same distance, because one: One second is too close: on a dry day you follow no closer than two seconds behind the car ahead. You slow down until you are at least two seconds behind, then count again at another sign post.
wrong.You speed up to stay close to the car ah: Speeding up brings you closer, and you already reached the sign post in less than two seconds. You slow down until you are at least two seconds behind.

steps.rule: Under normal conditions you follow no closer than two seconds, and when you reach the fixed point sooner, you slow down and check again until you are two seconds behind.

steps.prompt: You are driving on a state highway where the speed limit is 55 mph. It is a dry, clear day. You follow two seconds behind the car ahead. At what speeds on this road is two seconds enough?
options: Two seconds is enough at any speed on this road.
Two seconds is enough only up to 30 mph.
Two seconds is enough only up to 45 mph.
steps.answer: Two seconds is enough at any speed on this road.

then.say: Two seconds is enough at any speed on this road. The two-second rule holds at every speed on state and federal highways with moderate speed limits, like this one.

Two seconds is enough above 30 mph as well, and on this road you may drive up to 55 mph. On a state highway with a moderate speed limit, like this one, two seconds is enough at any speed.
Two seconds is enough above 45 mph as well, and on this road you may drive up to 55 mph. On a state highway with a moderate speed limit, like this one, two seconds is enough at any speed.

steps.rule: The two-second rule holds at any speed on state and U.S. highways with moderate speed limits.

steps.prompt: You are following a car on a state highway, and it is raining hard. What following distance do you keep?
options: You stay at least four seconds behind it.
You stay two seconds behind it, the same as on a dry day.
You stay one second behind it.
steps.answer: You stay at least four seconds behind it.

then.say: You stay at least four seconds behind it. Two seconds is not enough in bad weather, at night, or at higher speeds on the interstate. The extra distance lets you see more of the road ahead.

wrong.You stay two seconds behind it, the same: Two seconds is for normal conditions, and hard rain is bad weather. You stay at least four seconds behind the car ahead, which gives you more time to react.
One second is too close even on a dry day, when two seconds is the closest you follow. In hard rain you stay at least four seconds behind the car ahead.

steps.rule: In bad weather, at night, at higher interstate speeds, and behind a motorcycle, you follow at least four seconds behind the vehicle ahead.

steps.prompt: You are driving behind a motorcycle on a dry road in daylight. What following distance do you keep?
options: You stay at least four seconds behind it.
You stay two seconds behind it, the same as behind a car.
You stay one second behind it.
steps.answer: You stay at least four seconds behind it.

then.say: You stay at least four seconds behind it. Behind a motorcycle, two seconds is not enough, even on a dry road in daylight. The extra space gives you room to brake if the motorcycle stops suddenly.

wrong.You stay two seconds behind it, the same: Two seconds is for following a car in normal conditions, and behind a motorcycle you need more, even on a dry road in daylight. You stay at least four seconds behind it, which gives you room to brake if the motorcycle stops suddenly.
One second is too close even behind a car on a dry day, when two seconds is the closest you follow. Behind a motorcycle you stay at least four seconds back, which gives you room to brake if it stops suddenly.

steps.rule: In bad weather, at night, at higher interstate speeds, and behind a motorcycle, you follow at least four seconds behind the vehicle ahead.

steps.prompt: You are following a different car on a state highway and want to check how far behind it you are. The car ahead is about to pass a sign post at the side of the road. What do you do?
options: You count the seconds from when the car ahead passes the sign post until your car reaches it.
You count the cars between you and the sign post.
You guess how many car lengths are between you and the car ahead.
steps.answer: You count the seconds from when the car ahead passes the sign post until your car reaches it.

then.say: You count the seconds from when the car ahead passes the sign post until your car reaches it. The sign post stays in one place, so the seconds between the two cars passing it are your following distance. If you reach it before you finish “one-thousand and two”, you are too close.

wrong.You count the cars between you and the s: Counting cars does not tell you how far behind the car ahead you are. You count the seconds from when the car ahead passes the sign post until your car reaches it.
wrong.You guess how many car lengths are betwe: A guess does not measure anything. You count the seconds from when the car ahead passes the sign post until your car reaches it, because the sign post stays in one place.

steps.rule: To check your following distance, you count the seconds from when the car ahead passes a fixed point, such as a sign post, until you reach the same point.

steps.prompt: Rear-end crashes, where a car hits the back of the car ahead of it, are very common. Most of them are caused by drivers doing one thing. What is it?
options: The drivers follow too closely, which is called tailgating.
The drivers use their turn signals.
The drivers drive with their headlights on.
steps.answer: The drivers follow too closely, which is called tailgating.

then.say: Most rear-end crashes are caused by drivers who follow too closely, which is called tailgating. A driver who follows too closely cannot see the road past the car ahead, and has too little time to stop when it stops.

A turn signal tells the drivers around you what you plan to do, so using it does not cause a crash. Most rear-end crashes are caused by drivers who follow too closely, which is called tailgating.
wrong.The drivers drive with their headlights: Headlights make your car easier for other drivers to see, so driving with them on does not cause a crash. Most rear-end crashes are caused by drivers who follow too closely, which is called tailgating.

steps.rule: Most rear-end crashes are caused by drivers who follow too closely, which is called tailgating.

steps.prompt: You are driving past a school. A sign shows the speed limit for the school zone, which is lower than the limit on the rest of the road. When is that school zone speed limit in effect?
options: It is in effect when children are going to or from the school, or during a school recess.
It is in effect only from 7 a.m. to 9 a.m. on weekdays, all year.
It is in effect all day and all night, every day of the year.
steps.answer: It is in effect when children are going to or from the school, or during a school recess.

then.say: It is in effect when children are going to or from the school, or during a school recess. Those are the times children are near the road, so the lower limit applies then, not at set hours of the clock and not all the time.

Two hours in the morning leave out the time children go home from the school and the school recess. The school zone limit is in effect when children are going to or from the school, or during a school recess.
wrong.It is in effect all day and all night, e: The lower limit is not in effect all the time. It is in effect when children are going to or from the school, or during a school recess, because that is when children are near the road.

steps.rule: School zone speed limits are in effect when children are going to or from the school or during a school recess.

steps.prompt: Your car has anti-lock brakes, called ABS. The car ahead stops suddenly, and you must stop fast. How do you press the brake pedal?
options: You press it down firmly and hold it, without pumping.
You pump it quickly several times.
You press it, let it up, then press it again.
steps.answer: You press it down firmly and hold it, without pumping.

then.say: You press it down firmly and hold it, without pumping. Pumping the pedal or letting it up switches the anti-lock system off, so you keep steady pressure until the car stops. You may feel the pedal push back, which means the ABS is working.

Pumping the pedal switches the anti-lock system off. You press the pedal down firmly and hold it, with steady pressure, until the car stops.
wrong.You press it, let it up, then press it a: Letting the pedal up switches the anti-lock system off, the same as pumping it. You press the pedal down firmly and hold it, with steady pressure, until the car stops.

steps.rule: With anti-lock brakes, you press the brake pedal with firm, steady pressure and never pump it.

steps.prompt: You drove slower than 55 mph in the rain at night. You stayed four seconds behind a car in hard rain, and four seconds behind the motorcycle. What did driving slower and staying farther back give you?
options: They gave you more time to see a danger and react to it.
They gave you a shorter trip.
They gave you a better view of the cars behind you.
steps.answer: They gave you more time to see a danger and react to it.

then.say: The slower you drive and the farther back you stay, the more seconds you have before you reach a danger ahead, even though the trip takes longer. In those seconds you see the danger and brake or steer around it.

Driving slower and staying farther back make the trip longer, not shorter. They gave you more seconds to see a danger ahead and brake or steer around it.
wrong.They gave you a better view of the cars: Driving slower and staying farther back are about the road ahead of you, not the cars behind you. They gave you more seconds to see a danger ahead and brake or steer around it.

lessons.title: Stops you must make (school buses, trains, emergency vehicles, stop lines)

steps.prompt: You are coming up to a stop sign. A white stop line is painted across your lane. Where do you stop? Tap the place.

then.say: You stop behind the stop line. Past it, your car is out in the intersection, in the way of the cross traffic.

wrong.past: That puts your car out in the intersection, in the way of the cross traffic. You stop behind the stop line.

steps.rule: At a stop sign with a white stop line, you stop your vehicle behind the line.

steps.prompt: You are coming up to a stop sign. There is no stop line, but a crosswalk is painted across the road. Where do you stop? Tap the place.

then.say: You stop before the crosswalk, so your car is not where people walk across. Past it, your car is out in the intersection.

wrong.past: That puts your car out in the intersection, past where people walk across. With no stop line, you stop before the crosswalk.

steps.rule: At a stop sign with no stop line, you stop before the crosswalk, and with neither, before you enter the intersection, where you can see the cross traffic.

steps.prompt: You are coming up to a railroad crossing. No train is in sight. The red lights have just begun flashing, and the gate is still up. May you go across now?
options: Yes
No

then.say: No, you stop before the crossing, before the gate comes down. Flashing red lights mean a train is coming, even before you can see it.

wrong.Yes: Flashing red lights mean a train is coming, even when you cannot see it yet. You stop before the crossing, before the gate comes down.

steps.rule: At a crossing with lights and a gate, you stop when the lights begin flashing, before the gate comes down.

steps.prompt: A train is coming to the railroad crossing ahead, and the gate is down. How far from the tracks does Tennessee law say you must stop?
options: Between 15 and 50 feet from the tracks.
Between 5 and 10 feet from the tracks.
At least 100 feet from the tracks.
steps.answer: Between 15 and 50 feet from the tracks.

then.say: You stop between 15 and 50 feet from the tracks, and never on the tracks.

A stop 5 to 10 feet back is nearer to the tracks than the law allows. You stop between 15 and 50 feet from the tracks, and never on them.
A stop 100 feet back is farther from the tracks than the law allows. You stop between 15 and 50 feet from the tracks, and never on them.

steps.rule: When a train is coming, you stop between 15 and 50 feet from the railroad tracks, and never on the tracks.

steps.prompt: A train is coming to the railroad crossing ahead. A white stop line is painted across your lane, 30 feet from the tracks. Where do you stop? Tap the place.

then.say: You stop behind the stop line, 30 feet from the tracks, inside the 15 to 50 feet the law sets. On the tracks the train hits you, and 80 feet is farther back than the law allows.

wrong.on: That puts your car in the path of the train, and you never stop on the tracks. You stop behind the stop line, 30 feet from the tracks, inside the 15 to 50 feet the law sets.
wrong.at80: That far back is outside the 15 to 50 feet the law sets. You stop behind the stop line, 30 feet from the tracks.

steps.rule: At a railroad crossing with a stop line, you stop behind the stop line, which is painted between 15 and 50 feet from the tracks.

steps.prompt: You are stopped at the railroad crossing. The train has passed. The red lights are still flashing, and the gate is still down. May you go across now?
options: Yes
No

then.say: No, you stay stopped. Flashing lights and a lowered gate mean a train is coming, even after one has passed.

wrong.Yes: The lights are still flashing and the gate is still down, and that means a train is coming, even after one has passed. You stay stopped until the gate is up and the lights have stopped flashing.

steps.rule: At a crossing with lights and a gate, you stay stopped until the gates are raised and the lights stop flashing.

steps.prompt: You are stopped at the railroad crossing. The train has passed. The gate is up, and the red lights have stopped flashing. May you go across now?
options: Yes
No

then.say: Yes, you go across. You wait for both the gate to go up and the lights to stop, never only one.

wrong.No: Nothing keeps you stopped: the train has passed, the gate is up, and the red lights have stopped flashing. You go across.

steps.rule: At a crossing with lights and a gate, you may go across once the gates are raised and the lights have stopped flashing.

steps.prompt: You are driving behind a school bus. Its yellow lights are flashing. What do you do?
options: You slow down and get ready to stop.
You pass the bus before it stops.
You keep the same speed.
steps.answer: You slow down and get ready to stop.

then.say: You slow down and get ready to stop. Flashing yellow lights mean the bus is about to stop for children.

Flashing yellow lights mean the bus is about to stop to load or unload children, so you slow down instead of passing it. You get ready to stop behind it.
Flashing yellow lights mean the bus is about to stop to load or unload children, and at the same speed you are not ready to stop when it does. You slow down and get ready to stop.

steps.rule: When the yellow lights on a school bus are flashing, the bus is about to stop to load or unload children, so you slow down and get ready to stop.

steps.prompt: The school bus ahead has stopped. Its red lights are flashing and its stop arm is out. You have stopped behind it. When may you drive on?
options: When the red lights are off, the stop arm is pulled back, and the bus moves.
As soon as the children have reached the side of the road.
After you have waited 30 seconds.

wrong.near: That space is 5 feet from the crosswalk, and you may park no closer than 20 feet from a crosswalk. The space 20 feet from it is the closest you may use.
wrong.far: You may park there, but the law lets you park closer. You may park no closer than 20 feet from a crosswalk, so the space 20 feet from it is the closest you may use.

steps.rule: You may not park in a crosswalk or within 20 feet of one.

steps.prompt: You are the red car. The three spaces are 15, 30 and 50 feet from the stop sign. You want to park as close to it as the law allows. Which space do you use? Tap the space.

targets.label: the space 15 feet from the stop sign
the space 30 feet from the stop sign
the space 50 feet from the stop sign

then.say: You park in the space 30 feet from the stop sign. You may park no closer than 30 feet from a stop sign, a traffic signal or any other traffic control device. That keeps the sign in view for drivers coming up to it.

wrong.near: That space is 15 feet from the stop sign, and you may park no closer than 30 feet from a stop sign. The space 30 feet from it is the closest you may use.
wrong.far: You may park there, but the law lets you park closer. You may park no closer than 30 feet from a stop sign, so the space 30 feet from it is the closest you may use.

steps.rule: You may not park within 30 feet of a traffic signal, a stop sign or any other traffic control device.

steps.prompt: You are the red car. The three spaces are 20, 50 and 100 feet from the railroad crossing. You want to park as close to it as the law allows. Which space do you use? Tap the space.

targets.label: the space 20 feet from the railroad crossing
the space 50 feet from the railroad crossing
the space 100 feet from the railroad crossing

then.say: You park in the space 50 feet from the railroad crossing. You may park no closer than 50 feet from a railroad crossing, so that drivers coming up to it can see along the tracks.

wrong.near: That space is 20 feet from the railroad crossing, and you may park no closer than 50 feet from a railroad crossing. The space 50 feet from it is the closest you may use.
wrong.far: You may park there, but the law lets you park closer. You may park no closer than 50 feet from a railroad crossing, so the space 50 feet from it is the closest you may use.

steps.rule: You may not park within 50 feet of a railroad crossing.

steps.prompt: Where is it illegal to park?
options: It is illegal to park in a marked parking space.
It is illegal to park on a bridge or in a tunnel.
It is illegal to park 20 feet from a fire hydrant.
It is illegal to park in a parking lot.
steps.answer: It is illegal to park on a bridge or in a tunnel.

then.say: It is illegal to park on any bridge or in any tunnel, even at the edge of the road.

wrong.It is illegal to park in a marked parkin: A marked parking space is made for parking, so you may park in it, unless a sign reserves it for drivers with a disability. It is illegal to park on a bridge or in a tunnel.
wrong.It is illegal to park 20 feet from a fir: You may park 20 feet from a fire hydrant, because the law forbids parking within 15 feet of one, and 20 feet is farther than that. It is illegal to park on a bridge or in a tunnel.
A parking lot is made for parking, so you may park in it. It is illegal to park on a bridge or in a tunnel.

steps.rule: It is illegal to park on any bridge or in a tunnel.

steps.prompt: You are the red car. You have just parallel parked at the curb. How far from the curb should your car be?
options: Your car should be no more than 6 inches from the curb.
Your car should be no more than 12 inches from the curb.
Your car should be no more than 18 inches from the curb.
Your car should be no more than 24 inches from the curb.
steps.answer: Your car should be no more than 18 inches from the curb.

then.say: Your car should be no more than 18 inches from the curb. Farther out, it sticks into the lane where other cars drive past it.

wrong.Your car should be no more than 6 inches: The law allows more than 6 inches. Your car may be up to 18 inches from the curb, and no farther.
wrong.Your car should be no more than 12 inche: The law allows more than 12 inches. Your car may be up to 18 inches from the curb, and no farther.
wrong.Your car should be no more than 24 inche: At 24 inches your car sticks too far into the lane where other cars drive past it. Your car may be no more than 18 inches from the curb.

steps.rule: When you finish parallel parking, your car is no more than 18 inches from the curb.

steps.prompt: You are the red car. You are parked facing downhill, and there is a curb on your right. Which way do you turn your front wheels? Tap the wheels.

targets.label: the front wheels turned toward the curb
the front wheels turned away from the curb

then.say: You turn your front wheels toward the curb and set the parking brake. If the car rolls, it rolls into the curb and stops.

wrong.away: Turned away from the curb, the front wheels steer a rolling car out into the road and into traffic. You turn them toward the curb, so the car rolls into the curb and stops.

steps.rule: When you park facing downhill with a curb, you turn your front wheels toward the curb and set the parking brake.

steps.prompt: You are the red car. You are parked facing uphill, and there is a curb on your right. Which way do you turn your front wheels? Tap the wheels.

targets.label: the front wheels turned toward the curb
the front wheels turned away from the curb

then.say: You turn your front wheels away from the curb. If the car rolls back, the front wheel on the curb side catches the curb and the car stops, instead of rolling into traffic.

wrong.toward: Turned toward the curb, the front wheels steer the car away from the curb as it rolls back, out into the road and into traffic. You turn them away from the curb, so the front wheel catches the curb and the car stops.

steps.rule: When you park facing uphill with a curb, you turn your front wheels away from the curb, so a car that rolls back stops against the curb.

steps.prompt: You are the red car. You are parked facing downhill, and there is no curb. Which way do you turn your front wheels? Tap the wheels.

targets.label: the front wheels turned toward the edge of the road
the front wheels turned away from the edge of the road

then.say: You turn your front wheels toward the edge of the road. With no curb to stop it, a car that rolls goes off the road, away from traffic, instead of into it.

wrong.away: Turned away from the edge of the road, the front wheels steer a rolling car out into the road and into traffic. You turn them toward the edge of the road, so the car rolls off the road, away from traffic.

steps.rule: When you park facing downhill with no curb, you turn your front wheels toward the edge of the road, so the car rolls away from traffic.

steps.prompt: You are the red car. You are parked facing uphill, and there is no curb. Which way do you turn your front wheels? Tap the wheels.

targets.label: the front wheels turned toward the edge of the road
the front wheels turned away from the edge of the road

then.say: You turn your front wheels toward the edge of the road, the same as facing downhill with no curb. If the car rolls back, it goes off the road, away from traffic.

wrong.away: Turned away from the edge of the road, the front wheels let a car that rolls back go out toward the center of the road, into traffic. With no curb, uphill or downhill, you turn them toward the edge of the road.

steps.rule: When you park on a hill with no curb, uphill or downhill, you turn your front wheels toward the edge of the road, so the car rolls away from traffic.

steps.prompt: You are the red car, on the ramp. To merge is to move into a lane where traffic is already moving. You want to merge into the right lane of the interstate. What do you do?
options: You speed up on the ramp to the speed of the interstate traffic, then merge when the way is clear.
You stop at the end of the ramp, check for cars, then enter when it is safe.
You slow to 25 miles per hour before you enter the right lane.
You drive onto the shoulder first, then merge when the way is clear.
steps.answer: You speed up on the ramp to the speed of the interstate traffic, then merge when the way is clear.

then.say: You speed up on the ramp to the speed of the interstate traffic, then merge when the way is clear. Before you enter most busy roads you slow down or stop, but before you enter the interstate you do the opposite. Matching the speed of the cars in the lane lets you move in without making them brake.

wrong.You stop at the end of the ramp, check f: Stopping at the end of the ramp leaves you no room to reach the speed of the interstate traffic. Drivers behind you on the ramp do not expect you to stop and can hit you from behind. You speed up on the ramp, then merge when the way is clear.
wrong.You slow to 25 miles per hour before you: At 25 miles per hour you would enter the right lane far slower than the cars in it, and they could hit you from behind. You speed up on the ramp to the speed of the interstate traffic, then merge when the way is clear.
wrong.You drive onto the shoulder first, then: The shoulder is not a lane, and you do not drive on it to enter the interstate. You speed up on the ramp to the speed of the interstate traffic, then merge from the ramp when the way is clear.

steps.rule: When you enter the interstate, you use the ramp to speed up to the speed of the interstate traffic, then merge when the way is clear.

steps.prompt: You are the red car, on the ramp, and you want to merge into the right lane. The blue car is in that lane, coming up beside you. Who goes first? Tap the car.

then.say: The blue car goes first. You are entering the interstate, so you let the cars already on it go first and merge into a gap between them. Drivers on the interstate should make room for you when they can, but you do not count on it.

wrong.you: Your car is entering the interstate, and the cars already on it go first, whichever car is faster or larger. You let the blue car go by, then merge into the gap behind it.

steps.rule: When you merge onto the interstate from a ramp, you let the cars already on the interstate go first.

steps.prompt: You are the red car and driving slower than the other cars. Tap the lane you must use.

then.say: You use the right lane. On the interstate, a driver going slower than the flow of traffic must use the right lane, and the lanes to its left are for faster cars and passing.

wrong.left: The left lane is for passing and for the fastest cars, and a slow car there slows every car behind it. A driver going slower than the other cars must use the right lane.
wrong.middle: Staying in the middle lane keeps you in the way of faster cars, which then have to pass you on both sides. A driver going slower than the other cars must use the right lane.

steps.rule: On the interstate, if you drive slower than the flow of traffic, you must use the right lane.

steps.prompt: You are the red car, leaving the interstate at the exit ahead. The deceleration lane opens beside the right lane and leads to the exit. You want to slow down for the exit. Tap the lane you must use.

then.say: You keep your speed until you are in the deceleration lane, then slow to the ramp's posted speed. Slowing there keeps your car out of the way of the cars behind you in the right lane, which are still at interstate speed.

wrong.right: Slowing in the right lane puts you in the way of the cars behind you, which are still at interstate speed. You keep your speed until you are in the deceleration lane, then slow to the ramp's posted speed.

steps.rule: When you leave the interstate, you keep your speed until you enter the deceleration lane, then slow to the ramp's posted speed.

steps.prompt: You are the red car, and you have just driven past your exit. What must you do?
options: You go on to the next exit.
You back up on the shoulder to the exit.
You make a U-turn through the median.
You stop on the shoulder and wait.
steps.answer: You go on to the next exit.

then.say: You go on to the next exit and leave the interstate there. It is illegal to back up, make a U-turn, or cross the median on the interstate.

Backing up on the interstate is illegal, and it puts your car in the path of the cars coming up behind you at full speed. You go on to the next exit and leave the interstate there.
A U-turn on the interstate is illegal, and a U-turn through the median carries your car across the fast traffic going the other way. You go on to the next exit and leave the interstate there.
The shoulder is for emergencies, and a missed exit is not one. Waiting there does not bring you back to your exit, because you may not back up or turn around. You go on to the next exit and leave the interstate there.

steps.rule: If you miss your exit on the interstate, you must go on to the next exit.

steps.prompt: You are the red car. The gap in the median ahead is a crossover between the two sides of the interstate. Who may drive through it?
options: Only emergency vehicles and highway maintenance crews may drive through it.
Any driver who missed an exit and needs to turn around may drive through it.
Any driver may drive through it when no other cars are around.
Trucks and buses that need to turn around may drive through it.
steps.answer: Only emergency vehicles and highway maintenance crews may drive through it.

then.say: Only emergency vehicles and highway maintenance crews may drive through it. Every other driver, you included, may never cross the median, even where there is a gap.

wrong.Any driver who missed an exit and needs: Missing an exit does not allow a driver to cross the median. Only emergency vehicles and highway maintenance crews may drive through it, and a driver who missed an exit goes on to the next exit.
wrong.Any driver may drive through it when no: An empty road does not change who may cross the median. Only emergency vehicles and highway maintenance crews may drive through it, at any time.
wrong.Trucks and buses that need to turn aroun: Trucks and buses may not cross the median any more than your car may. Only emergency vehicles and highway maintenance crews may drive through it.

steps.rule: Only emergency vehicles and highway maintenance crews may cross an interstate median.

steps.prompt: You are the red car. The white car is an emergency vehicle stopped on the right shoulder with its lights flashing, and no car is near you in the left lane. Tap the lane you must use.

then.say: You move into the left lane, which is not next to the stopped vehicle. The Move Over law requires you to change to a lane not next to a stopped emergency vehicle with its lights flashing, when you can do it safely. That keeps your car away from anyone working beside it.

wrong.right: The right lane is next to the stopped emergency vehicle, and anyone working beside it is a few feet from that lane. The Move Over law requires you to change to a lane not next to it when you can do it safely, so you move into the left lane.

steps.rule: When you come up to an emergency vehicle stopped with its lights flashing, you change to a lane not next to it, or slow down and drive with caution if you cannot.

steps.prompt: You are the red car. The white car is an emergency vehicle stopped on the right shoulder with its lights flashing. The blue car beside you keeps you from moving into the left lane. What do you do?
options: You slow down and drive past it with caution in your lane.
You stop behind it and wait until it drives away.
You honk your horn and keep going at the same speed.
You turn on your high beams and pass it quickly.
steps.answer: You slow down and drive past it with caution in your lane.

then.say: You slow down and drive past it with caution in your lane. The Move Over law requires you to change to a lane not next to the stopped vehicle. When you cannot do that safely, you slow down and drive with caution instead.

wrong.You stop behind it and wait until it dri: The law does not ask you to stop, and stopping on the interstate puts your car in the way of the fast traffic behind you. When you cannot move over safely, you slow down and drive past it with caution.
wrong.You honk your horn and keep going at the: Honking does not protect anyone working beside the emergency vehicle, and keeping your speed takes you past them close and fast. When you cannot move over safely, you slow down and drive past it with caution.
wrong.You turn on your high beams and pass it: High beams can blind anyone working there, and passing quickly is the opposite of what the law requires. When you cannot move over safely, you slow down and drive past it with caution.

steps.rule: When you come up to an emergency vehicle stopped with its lights flashing, you change to a lane not next to it, or slow down and drive with caution if you cannot.

steps.prompt: You are the red car. The orange diamond sign warns that the right lane is closed ahead for road work, and no car is near you in the left lane. Tap the lane you must use.

then.say: You merge into the left lane now, as soon as you see the work zone. Merging early keeps the traffic moving at the posted speed, and no driver is forced over at the last moment.

wrong.right: The right lane is open until the cones, but waiting until the last moment to merge can get you a ticket and can cause a crash. You merge into the left lane as soon as you see the work zone.

steps.rule: When a lane is closed ahead in a work zone, you merge out of it as soon as you see the work zone, not at the last moment.

steps.prompt: You are the red car, and your engine is losing power. What do you do first?
options: You move to the right shoulder and turn on your emergency flashers.
You stop where you are in your lane and turn on your emergency flashers.
You move to the left shoulder and turn off your lights.
You keep driving slowly in the right lane.
steps.answer: You move to the right shoulder and turn on your emergency flashers.

then.say: You move to the right shoulder as soon as you can and turn on your emergency flashers, which make all your turn signal lights flash at once. The shoulder takes your car out of the fast traffic, and the flashers warn other drivers that your car is stopped there.

wrong.You stop where you are in your lane and: A car stopped in a lane of the interstate can be hit from behind by traffic at full speed, even with its emergency flashers on. You move to the right shoulder as soon as you can, then turn on your emergency flashers, which make all your turn signal lights flash at once.
wrong.You move to the left shoulder and turn o: The left shoulder is beside the fastest lane, and with your lights off other drivers cannot see your car. You move to the right shoulder and turn on your emergency flashers, which make all your turn signal lights flash to warn other traffic.
wrong.You keep driving slowly in the right lan: A car far below the speed of traffic is in the way of every car behind it, and your engine may stop while you are still in the lane. You move to the right shoulder as soon as you can and turn on your emergency flashers, which make all your turn signal lights flash at once.

steps.rule: If your car has trouble on the interstate, you move to the right shoulder as soon as you can and turn on your emergency flashers.

steps.prompt: You are the red car. Safe interstate driving demands complete awareness of driving at higher speed. What else does it demand?
options: It demands constant alertness by the driver.
It demands a car with a large engine.
It demands driving in the left lane at all times.
It demands keeping up with the fastest car.
steps.answer: It demands constant alertness by the driver.

then.say: It demands constant alertness by the driver. At interstate speed the cars around you change lanes, merge and brake within seconds. You keep watching the road ahead, your mirrors and the cars beside you the whole time.

The size of the engine does not make a driver safe. Safe interstate driving demands constant alertness by the driver, along with awareness of driving at higher speed.
wrong.It demands driving in the left lane at a: The left lane is for passing and for the fastest cars, not for driving in at all times. Safe interstate driving demands constant alertness by the driver.
wrong.It demands keeping up with the fastest c: You keep pace with the traffic, but you never speed to stay with the fastest car. Safe interstate driving demands constant alertness by the driver.

steps.rule: Safe interstate driving demands complete awareness of driving at higher speed and constant alertness by the driver.

steps.prompt: You are the red car, driving at night with your low beams on. A person in dark clothes is walking at the roadside, past the end of your headlight beams. Can you see the person yet?

No

then.say: You cannot see the person yet. At night you see only as far as your headlights light the road, and the person is past the end of the beams.

wrong.Yes: Your headlights do not light the road where the person is walking, past the end of the beams. At night you see only as far as your headlights light the road, so you cannot see the person yet.

steps.rule: Driving at night is more dangerous than driving in the daytime, because your headlights limit how far you can see.

steps.prompt: How does driving at night compare with driving in the daytime?
options: It is safer, because there is less traffic.
It is safer, so you can drive faster.

wrong.It is safer, because there is less traff: There is less traffic at night, but the chance of a serious crash is much greater than in the daytime. Your headlights limit how far you can see, so driving at night is more dangerous.

wrong.It is just as safe, as long as your ligh: Even with your lights on, the distance you can see clearly at night is greatly reduced. Driving at night is more dangerous, because your headlights limit how far you can see.

steps.rule: Driving at night is more dangerous than driving in the daytime, because your headlights limit how far you can see.

steps.prompt: You are driving, and the sun set 30 minutes ago. Does the law require your headlights to be on now?

No

steps.rule: By law your headlights must be on from 30 minutes after sunset until 30 minutes before sunrise.

steps.prompt: By law, when must your headlights be on at night?
options: They must be on from sunset until sunrise.
They must be on from 30 minutes after sunset until 30 minutes before sunrise.
They must be on from 1 hour after sunset until 1 hour before sunrise.
They must be on from 15 minutes after sunset until 15 minutes before sunrise.

wrong.They must be on from sunset until sunris: The law does not start the time at sunset or end it at sunrise. Your headlights must be on from 30 minutes after sunset until 30 minutes before sunrise.
wrong.They must be on from 1 hour after sunset: The law's time is 30 minutes, not 1 hour, so waiting 1 hour after sunset leaves your headlights off when they must be on. They must be on from 30 minutes after sunset until 30 minutes before sunrise.
wrong.They must be on from 15 minutes after su: The law's time is 30 minutes, not 15 minutes. Your headlights must be on from 30 minutes after sunset until 30 minutes before sunrise.

steps.rule: By law your headlights must be on from 30 minutes after sunset until 30 minutes before sunrise.

steps.prompt: You are the red car, driving at night with your high beams on. The blue car coming toward you is 500 feet away, and the green car behind it is 1,000 feet away. Which car is close enough that you must dim your high beams for it? Tap the car.

then.say: You dim your high beams for the blue car. You must dim them when you meet a vehicle within 500 feet, about the length of one city block. Their glare can blind the other driver.

wrong.far: The green car is 1,000 feet away, and you must dim your high beams for a vehicle within 500 feet, so it is not close enough yet. The blue car is 500 feet away, so you dim them for it now.

steps.rule: At night you must dim your high beams when you meet or overtake a vehicle within 500 feet.

steps.prompt: You are the red car, driving at night with your high beams on. You are following the blue car, 500 feet behind it. Do you dim your high beams?
options: Yes
No

then.say: You dim your high beams when you follow a vehicle within 500 feet. The glare of your high beams in the blue car's mirrors can blind its driver.

wrong.No: The glare of your high beams in the blue car's mirrors can blind its driver. You dim your high beams when you follow a vehicle within 500 feet, and the blue car is 500 feet ahead.

steps.rule: At night you must dim your high beams when you meet, follow or overtake a vehicle within 500 feet.

steps.prompt: You are driving in fog at night. Which lights do you use?
options: You use your high beams.
You use your parking lights only.
You use your fog lights only.
You use your low beams.

then.say: You use your low beams. In fog, the light of high beams reflects off the fog back into your eyes. Low beams put the light on the road, so you see better and other drivers see you.

In fog, the light of your high beams reflects off the fog back into your eyes, so you see less. You use your low beams, which put the light on the road and help other drivers see you.
Driving with only your parking lights on in fog is against the law, because their small size can make other drivers think your car is farther away than it is. You use your low beams, which put the light on the road and help other drivers see you.
Driving with only your fog lights on is against the law. You use your low beams, which put the light on the road and help other drivers see you.

steps.rule: In fog you use your low beams, because they let you see better and help other drivers see you.

steps.prompt: Your car starts to hydroplane on a wet road: its tires ride up on a layer of water and lose their grip on the road. What do you do?
options: You slow down gradually by letting up on the gas.
You slam on the brakes.
You speed up a little to push through the water.
You turn the steering wheel sharply to one side.
steps.answer: You slow down gradually by letting up on the gas.

then.say: You let up on the gas and slow down gradually. While the tires ride on the water, they do not have the grip to steer or to brake. Hard braking or a sharp turn can make the car skid or spin.

The tires riding on the water have no grip to brake with, so slamming on the brakes can make the car skid. You slow down gradually by letting up on the gas.
wrong.You speed up a little to push through th: Hydroplaning is more likely at higher speed, so speeding up makes it worse. You slow down gradually by letting up on the gas.
wrong.You turn the steering wheel sharply to o: The tires riding on the water have no grip to steer with, and a sharp turn can make the car skid or spin. You slow down gradually by letting up on the gas.

steps.rule: If your car starts to hydroplane, you slow down gradually by letting up on the gas.

steps.prompt: You are the red car, and your car does not have anti-lock brakes. The rear of your car is sliding to the left. Which way do you turn the steering wheel? Tap the steering wheel.

targets.label: the steering wheel turned to the left
the steering wheel turned to the right

then.say: You turn the steering wheel to the left, the way the rear of your car is sliding. That brings the front of the car back in line with the rear and straightens it. As soon as the car begins to straighten, you turn the steering wheel back so that the car does not swing the other way.

wrong.right: Turning the steering wheel to the right, away from the way the rear is sliding, does not bring the front of the car back in line with the rear. You turn the steering wheel to the left, the way the rear is sliding, and the car straightens.

steps.rule: Without anti-lock brakes, when your car starts to skid you take your foot off the brake and turn the steering wheel in the direction of the skid.

steps.prompt: You are the red car, and your car does not have anti-lock brakes. The rear of your car is sliding to the left, and your foot is on the brake. What do you do with the brake?
options: You press the brake harder.
You pump the brake.
You take your foot off the brake.
You keep the brake pressed as it is.
steps.answer: You take your foot off the brake.

then.say: You take your foot off the brake and steer in the direction of the skid. Until the car slows, the brakes do not work and can make the car skid more. Wheels that roll let you steer the car back in line.

Until the car slows, the brakes do not work, and pressing harder can make the car skid more. You take your foot off the brake and steer in the direction of the skid.
Pumping the brake is still braking, and until the car slows, braking can make the car skid more. You take your foot off the brake and steer in the direction of the skid.
Until the car slows, the brakes do not work, and keeping them pressed can make the car skid more. You take your foot off the brake and steer in the direction of the skid.

steps.rule: Without anti-lock brakes, when your car starts to skid you take your foot off the brake and turn the steering wheel in the direction of the skid.

steps.prompt: You are driving on snow and ice. What does braking hard and keeping the pedal down often do?
options: It stops the car faster on the ice.
It locks the front wheels, so you lose steering control.
It keeps the brakes warm, so they do not freeze.
It makes the tires grip the road better.
steps.answer: It locks the front wheels, so you lose steering control.

then.say: It locks the front wheels, and front wheels that do not roll cannot steer the car, so you lose steering control. You keep your speed low enough for snow and ice that you never need to brake hard.

Braking hard on ice locks the front wheels, and locked wheels slide on the ice instead of gripping it. You lose steering control, so you keep a speed at which you never need to brake hard.
wrong.It keeps the brakes warm, so they do not: Holding the brake down does not protect the brakes from the cold. It locks the front wheels, and front wheels that do not roll cannot steer, so you lose steering control.
Braking hard on ice does the opposite: it locks the front wheels, and locked wheels slide instead of gripping the road. You lose steering control.

steps.rule: Braking hard and keeping the pedal down on snow and ice can lock the front wheels, so you lose steering control.

steps.prompt: You are the red car, and flood water covers the road ahead of you. What do you do?
options: You drive through slowly in low gear.
You drive through quickly to keep your speed up.
You follow another car through the water.
You turn around and find another way.
steps.answer: You turn around and find another way.

then.say: You turn around and find another way. The water may be deeper than it looks, and the road under it may be washed out. Even a heavy car floats in moving water.

Driving slowly does not keep your car from floating, and the road under the water may be washed out. You turn around and find another way.
wrong.You drive through quickly to keep your s: Speed does not keep your car on the road, and the water may be deeper than it looks. You turn around and find another way.
wrong.You follow another car through the water: Another car getting through does not make the water safe for yours, and the road under it may be washed out. You turn around and find another way.
